ML Framework Modules

Install Blog GitHub

Gollek ML Framework Modules

This page replaces the older “SDK modules” view.

Gollek is moving toward a Gradle-only module layout with:

  • ml/* for the Java ML framework itself
  • trainer/* for training lifecycle and orchestration
  • integration/* for JBang, Jupyter, LangChain4j, and other adapters

Older gollek-sdk-* names still appear in some examples and historical docs, but they should be treated as compatibility surfaces during the migration, not the canonical structure.

This page intentionally stays at /docs/sdk-modules.md so older links do not break, but the content is now about the broader Gollek platform module naming, not just the SDK layer.

Build and Install Path

For local development installs on macOS, use:

  • ./run-install-local-macos.sh

This path now runs a Gradle-only install flow by default. Legacy Maven command fallback is intentionally removed from the default installer path to keep build behavior consistent.

Platform Naming Rules

Gollek should use distinct naming families for distinct responsibilities.

Family Canonical naming Purpose
Inference and serving gollek-backend-*, gollek-runner-*, gollek-plugin-runner-*, gollek-provider-*, gollek-spi-* runtime engine, hardware adapters, format runners, serving contracts
Client and application SDK gollek-sdk-* application-facing SDKs, sessions, local/remote client access
Java ML framework gollek-ml-* model building, data, optimization, export, hub, framework utilities
Trainer gollek-trainer-* training lifecycle, experiment orchestration, trainer runtime contracts
Integrations gollek-integration-* JBang, Jupyter, LangChain4j, and other adapters

Jupyter Integration

The Jupyter adapter is documented as gollek-integration-jupyter. It is a standalone Gollek Java kernel with preloaded ML helpers, rich notebook outputs, dependency magics, and artifact-inspection commands such as %tree, %du, %zipls, %tarls, %extract, and %sha256. Its CSV/TSV magics also support dataframe-style previews with -n row limits, --profile column stats, %sample random row checks, %sort top/bottom row previews, %filter row subsets, %describe numeric summaries, %schema dtype-style inference, %missing missingness checks, %valuecounts categorical counts, %scatter relationship checks, %groupby grouped summaries, %lineplot inline SVG trends, and %hist distribution checks, plus %corr --heatmap Pearson correlation matrices from CSV/TSV artifacts.

That split matches the Gollek vision:

  • inference/serving is the core identity
  • Java ML/training is a first-class framework layer
  • SDKs and integrations are adapters around those cores, not the core itself

Inference and Serving

For the serving side, prefer these naming patterns:

  • backend/*
    • hardware-specific acceleration surfaces such as Metal, CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan
  • runner/*
    • model-format execution adapters such as GGUF, Safetensor, ONNX, LiteRT
  • provider/* and spi/*
    • provider routing and runtime contracts
  • sdk/*
    • application-facing client access, not the ML framework itself

Architecture naming should also stay explicit:

  • native-java
    • preferred long-term path where Gollek handles execution in Java directly
  • binding
    • short-term compatibility and fallback path for llama.cpp, libtorch, LiteRT, ONNX runtime, and similar native bridges

For mobile and portable library usage, the most natural naming surfaces are:

  • :runner:onnx:*
  • :runner:litert:*

Those are the right places to emphasize Quarkus/GraalVM portability and platform-specific delivery.

Canonical Layout

Core ML Framework

Canonical Gradle module Role
:ml:gollek-ml-api umbrella framework entrypoint
:ml:gollek-ml-core shared estimator and transformer foundations
:ml:gollek-ml-selection metrics, cross-validation, model selection
:ml:gollek-ml-data dataset and dataloader APIs
:ml:gollek-ml-diffusion-api diffusion-training contracts for Java task, prompt, scheduler, and session APIs
:ml:gollek-ml-diffusion-opd Java implementation scaffold for DiffusionOPD-style multi-task distillation
:ml:gollek-ml-runner-api runner abstraction for ONNX, LiteRT, and future adapters

For diffusion alignment, Gollek now exposes a Java-first OPD surface described in:

  • DiffusionOPD in Gollek

Current public training data and metric conveniences live behind tech.kayys.gollek.ml.Gollek.DL:

  • TrainingPreset.REGRESSION_HUBER_*, huberLoss(...), and trainingOptions().regressionMetrics() support outlier-tolerant regression with MAE, MSE, RMSE, and R2 reporting.
  • trainingOptions().checkpointDir(...).restoreBestModelAtEnd() saves validation-driven best-model snapshots to canonical-best-model.safetensors and reloads the best epoch before returning. By default the monitor is validation loss, but .bestModelMonitorMetric("f1", BestModelMonitorMode.MAX) can select by a named validation metric such as F1, accuracy, AUROC, or average precision.
  • trainingOptions().earlyStopping(...).earlyStoppingMonitorMetric(...) uses the same validation metric stream to stop by task quality, so classification runs can stop on F1 or AUROC while regression runs keep the validation-loss default.
  • TrainingSummary.metadata().get("epochHistory") gives one row per completed epoch with train/validation losses, metric values, learning rate, optimizer steps, and scheduler steps for dashboards and reproducible debugging.
  • trainingOptions().stepLrBatches(...), .cosineAnnealingLrBatches(...), .warmupCosineLrBatches(...), and their Epochs variants expose public scheduler policies for one-call fit(...). Warmup/cosine starts new runs at LR 0.0, supports scheduler checkpoint resume, and reports learningRateSchedulerState.* metadata.
  • trainingOptions().reduceLrOnPlateauValidationLoss(...) lowers LR when validation loss stalls, while .reduceLrOnPlateauMetric(...) can follow a named validation metric. Plateau state is checkpointed and reported through learningRateSchedulerState.*.
  • Summary and history metadata include gradient/parameter diagnostics such as latestGradientL2NormBeforeClip, latestGradientL2Norm, latestGradientClipped, and latestParameterL2Norm, making exploding or clipped gradients visible in ordinary SDK runs.
  • The trainer has a non-finite guard for NaN/Inf loss and gradients. It fails before unsafe backward/optimizer updates, clears pending gradients, avoids writing corrupted checkpoints, and reports nonFinite* metadata plus a stopReason such as non-finite-train-loss.
  • Summary and history metadata also include train/validation throughput counters such as trainBatchCount, trainSampleCount, trainSamplesPerSecond, validationBatchCount, and validationSamplesPerSecond.
  • When checkpointDir(...) is set, the same history is persisted as canonical-history.csv beside the checkpoint files for spreadsheet-friendly learning-curve inspection. Resumed runs reload existing rows and append new epochs so interrupted training keeps a continuous curve. Nested metric maps and detailed diagnostics are encoded as deterministic JSON cells, so dashboards can parse confusion matrices and similar payloads without scraping Java Map.toString() text. Malformed structured cells are surfaced through trainingHistoryLoadError and rejected by strict resume. Duplicate headers, blank headers, and rows with extra cells are treated as ambiguous history shape errors instead of being silently overwritten or ignored. The epoch column is required and must contain unique non-negative integers.
  • The checkpoint directory also receives canonical-report.json, a structured trainer report with final summary fields, epoch history, metric maps, checkpoint state, accelerator metadata, gradient diagnostics, and throughput counters for CLIs, dashboards, and JBang examples.
  • Optimizer checkpoints now preserve SGD momentum, Adam/AdamW moments, and RMSprop accumulators/velocity so resumeFromCheckpoint() can continue optimizer dynamics instead of only restoring model weights.
  • Optimizers and GradientClipper now validate finite hyperparameters, parameter values, and gradients before mutating state. Adam L2 weight decay leaves gradient buffers intact, and Adagrad applies weight decay uniformly across the full tensor.
  • StepLR, CosineAnnealingLR, WarmupCosineScheduler, and ReduceLROnPlateau now validate finite scheduler configuration and checkpoint payloads before restoring resumed learning rates, rejecting NaN LRs, negative counters, and infinite plateau metrics.
  • Trainer summaries now expose partial-resume diagnostics for checkpoint artifacts, so users can see whether model, optimizer, scheduler, GradScaler, or history files were missing when resume began even if the run recreates them later. Strict resume now fails closed on missing runtime state or required artifacts, while lenient loading records checkpointResumePartial and the missing names.
  • Model checkpoints now write canonical-model.metadata beside canonical-model.safetensors. Resume validates model class and parameter signatures plus byte-size/SHA-256 integrity when metadata exists, fails fast by default on incompatible or corrupted snapshots, and records checkpointResumeCompatibilityMismatches when lenient checkpoint loading is explicitly enabled.
  • Checkpoint directories now also write canonical-checkpoints.metadata, a byte-size/SHA-256 manifest for runtime, optimizer, scheduler, GradScaler, history, report, and model artifacts. Resume validates runtime-state files before deserializing them, so corrupted runtime/optimizer/scheduler state fails closed by default and is reported through lenient compatibility diagnostics. Best-model restore-at-end uses the same manifest guard before replacing current weights.
  • Train and validation batches now validate non-null, non-empty, sample-aligned, finite input/label tensors before forward or loss execution, so malformed or NaN/Infinity dataset values fail before they can poison gradients, optimizer state, or validation metrics.
  • Custom trainer loss functions must return a single-value tensor. Vector or matrix losses now fail before backward(), surfacing invalidLossShape instead of logging one value while autograd propagates another reduction.
  • Trainer model outputs are validated before loss and metric evaluation, so NaN/Infinity predictions fail as nonFiniteKind=prediction instead of leaking into custom losses or validation metrics.
  • Trainer metric snapshots now validate finite values after real train/validation batches have run. Duplicate names, NaN/Infinity, or throwing custom metrics stop the run, and DetailedMetric payloads are guarded the same way. Failures report invalidMetric* metadata and skip final checkpoint writes, while empty train/validation phases may remain undefined for compatibility.
  • Trainer metric contracts are now standalone TrainingMetric and DetailedTrainingMetric APIs, with TrainingMetrics as the public built-in catalog. Built-ins are split internally by regression, binary, multiclass, and multilabel metric families. The legacy CanonicalTrainer.Metric, .DetailedMetric, and .Metrics names remain as compatibility aliases instead of owning the implementation.
  • QuantizationEngine now uses real supplied weights: either direct in-memory tensors or a simple text weight file. Missing model files fail fast instead of generating placeholder weights, and the output artifact includes quantized codes, dequantized values, compression estimates, and error metrics.
  • GradScaler now performs real mixed-precision loss scaling: callers backpropagate the returned scaled loss, unscale optimizer/parameter gradients, skip unsafe steps on NaN/Inf, and let the scale grow/back off from observed overflow. The scaler can now be checkpointed/resumed with compatibility validation and overflow-safe unscale writes.
  • CanonicalTrainer.Builder.mixedPrecision(true), .gradScaler(...), and trainingOptions().mixedPrecision() now use that scaler during the actual trainer step. Public trainingOptions().gradScaler(customScaler) / .mixedPrecision(customScaler) can tune the initial scale and growth policy, while overflowed updates are skipped and canonical-grad-scaler.state persists scaler state for resume. Incompatible saved scaler policies fail closed by default, with opt-in lenient loading surfacing the mismatch in trainer metadata and gradScalerCheckpointFallbackUsed.
  • GradTensor now differentiates common composed training graphs including view ops, sum/mean, pow, unary math/activation ops, and last-dimension softmax, so custom Java losses can rely on autograd instead of manual hooks for basic expressions.
  • Gollek.cat(...), Gollek.stack(...), and Gollek.where(...) now keep autograd links alive through concatenation, stacking, and broadcasted selection paths.
  • Transformer attention compatibility einsums (bhid,bhjd->bhij and bhij,bhjd->bhid) now keep gradients connected through attention score and context application paths for Java-side transformer training.
  • Public MultiHeadAttention keeps gradients through head split/merge reshapes and causal masks, and TransformerBlock dropout now applies a differentiable mask instead of returning detached tensors.
  • FlashAttention uses differentiable exact attention when gradients are tracked, while the no-grad tiled inference path keeps its memory-efficient loop and correctly merges multi-head output order.
  • MultiHeadAttention(..., dropoutP) now applies attention-probability dropout after softmax, and transformer encoder/decoder layers pass their dropout setting into internal self/cross attention modules.
  • TransformerBlock now uses a registered GELU feed-forward activation, so the implementation matches the documented transformer FFN instead of silently behaving like a ReLU block.
  • RotaryEmbedding.apply(...) now keeps RoPE gradients connected via the inverse rotation and validates rank, head dimension, and max sequence length before using the frequency cache.
  • Root tech.kayys.gollek.ml.nn.GroupNorm now preserves gradients through differentiable reshape/mean/variance tensor ops and validates group/channel configuration before training.
  • Dropout now rejects non-finite probabilities and handles p=1 as an explicit zero-output/zero-gradient path, while layer GroupNorm validates group counts, epsilon, rank, and channel count.
  • Weighted CrossEntropyLoss now uses sample-weight mean normalization for both scalar loss and logits gradients instead of scaling by raw batch size.
  • CrossEntropy, Focal, LabelSmoothing, ArcFace, and CTC losses now validate class-index targets so wrongly-shaped, NaN, fractional, or out-of-range labels fail before training indexes logits.
  • CrossEntropy, LabelSmoothing, BCE-with-logits, and focal losses now reject non-finite logits before softmax/sigmoid loss computation, preventing bad activations from entering the trainer graph as silent NaN gradients.
  • FocalLoss and BinaryFocalWithLogitsLoss now reject empty or non-finite logits before focal weighting, with finite-difference coverage for positive-weighted binary/multi-label focal gradients.
  • Regression losses (MSELoss, L1Loss, SmoothL1Loss, HuberLoss) now reject empty tensors and NaN/Inf predictions or targets before loss/gradient computation, and SmoothL1Loss uses standard beta-scaled semantics.
  • LabelSmoothingLoss now keeps gradients connected with the standard softmax - smoothedTarget backward path for calibrated classification training.
  • BCEWithLogitsLoss now uses a stable softplus formulation, preserving large losses for confident wrong binary predictions and rejecting non-finite logits or invalid targets before training.
  • DiceLoss now backpropagates the overlap objective for segmentation training and validates probability predictions, binary masks, matching shapes, and smoothing values.
  • IoULoss now backpropagates through predicted bounding boxes and validates [batch, 4] finite, ordered coordinates before computing object-detection overlap loss.
  • TripletLoss now backpropagates active margin violations to anchor, positive, and negative embeddings and validates matching [batch, dim] embedding tensors.
  • ContrastiveLoss now backpropagates positive pairs and active negative margin violations while validating binary labels and matching [batch, dim] embedding tensors.
  • CosineEmbeddingLoss now backpropagates positive and active negative cosine pairs while validating strict 1.0/-1.0 labels, margin bounds, and matching [batch, dim] embedding tensors.
  • CTCLoss now backpropagates log-probability inputs using log-space forward-backward posteriors and rejects blank/impossible target alignments before training.
  • ArcFaceLoss now backpropagates through feature embeddings and learned class centers, including normalization and angular-margin derivatives.
  • KnowledgeDistillation now trains student models from both soft teacher distributions and hard labels using teacher-to-student KL plus CrossEntropy, with teacher logits detached and student gradients preserved.
  • The default CPU NN backend now implements depthwise convolution, image resize/crop/normalize, scaled dot-product attention, and multi-head attention instead of returning null for these runtime paths.
  • classificationDataLoader(...) and classificationTrainValidationSplit(...) accept Java int[] labels and produce CrossEntropy-compatible class-index tensors.
  • classificationStratifiedTrainValidationSplit(...) and binaryStratifiedTrainValidationSplit(...) preserve class/binary label coverage across train and validation sets for small classification datasets.
  • multiLabelBinaryStratifiedTrainValidationSplit(...) balances per-label positive counts while preserving exact train/validation sizes for multi-label BCE datasets.
  • trainingOptions().classificationMetrics() records accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1 into TrainingSummary.metadata().
  • confusionMatrixMetric() / trainingOptions().confusionMatrixMetric() records scalar confusion_matrix_accuracy plus structured matrix details in summary metadata, epoch history, canonical-history.csv, and canonical-report.json. Rows represent actual classes and columns represent predicted classes.
  • trainingOptions().topKAccuracyMetric(k) records top-k accuracy, such as top2_accuracy or top5_accuracy, for logits shaped [batch, classes].
  • classificationMacroRocAucMetric(), classificationMacroAveragePrecisionMetric(), and trainingOptions().classificationRankingMetrics() report one-vs-rest multi-class ranking quality directly from CrossEntropy-style logits.
  • classWeights(...) derives balanced weights for imbalanced multi-class datasets, classWeightsFor(numClasses, ...) supports explicit class counts, and trainingOptions().crossEntropyClassWeights(...) applies those weights to the one-call CrossEntropy trainer preset path.
  • TrainingPreset.CLASSIFICATION_FOCAL_*, focalLoss(...), and trainingOptions().focalGamma(...) / .focalClassWeights(...) support focal-loss classification for hard-example-focused imbalanced training, with finite-logit validation before softmax/focal weighting.
  • TrainingPreset.BINARY_FOCAL_WITH_LOGITS_*, binaryFocalWithLogitsLoss(...), and trainingOptions().focalGamma(...) / .focalAlpha(...) combine focal hard-example weighting with existing .bcePositiveWeight(...) / .bcePositiveWeights(...) controls for imbalanced binary and multi-label training, with finite-logit validation and tested positive-weight gradients.
  • binaryDataLoader(...), binaryTrainValidationSplit(...), binaryStratifiedTrainValidationSplit(...), and TrainingPreset.BINARY_BCE_WITH_LOGITS_* support one-output binary classifiers using BCE-with-logits targets shaped [batch, 1].
  • binaryPositiveWeight(...) derives negatives / positives for imbalanced binary datasets, and trainingOptions().bcePositiveWeight(...) applies it to the one-call BCE trainer preset path.
  • trainingOptions().binaryClassificationMetrics() records thresholded binary accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 using logit 0.0 as the probability 0.5 boundary.
  • binaryAccuracyMetric(logitThreshold), binaryF1Metric(logitThreshold), and trainingOptions().binaryClassificationMetrics(logitThreshold) evaluate binary BCE/focal logits at deployment-specific operating points.
  • binaryConfusionMatrixMetric(logitThreshold) and trainingOptions().binaryConfusionMatrixMetric(logitThreshold) record scalar binary_confusion_matrix_accuracy plus TN/FP/FN/TP, specificity, balanced accuracy, and a structured [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]] matrix in trainer summaries, evaluation summaries, epoch history, and reports.
  • binaryRocAucMetric(), binaryAveragePrecisionMetric(), and trainingOptions().binaryRankingMetrics() report ranking quality directly from logits for imbalanced binary datasets.
  • multiLabelBinaryDataLoader(...), multiLabelBinaryTrainValidationSplit(...), and multiLabelBinaryStratifiedTrainValidationSplit(...) accept Java int[][], boolean[][], or float[][] targets while preserving [batch, labels] shape for multi-label BCE training.
  • multiLabelPositiveWeights(...) derives per-label imbalance weights, and trainingOptions().bcePositiveWeights(...) applies those weights to multi-label BCE-with-logits presets.
  • trainingOptions().multiLabelBinaryMetrics() records exact-match accuracy, Hamming loss, macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1 for multi-label BCE outputs.
  • multiLabelMacroF1Metric(logitThreshold) and trainingOptions().multiLabelBinaryMetrics(logitThreshold) evaluate multi-label BCE/focal logits with custom thresholds when probability 0.5 is not the desired operating point.
  • multiLabelMacroRocAucMetric(), multiLabelMacroAveragePrecisionMetric(), and trainingOptions().multiLabelRankingMetrics() report per-label macro ranking quality directly from multi-label logits.
  • evaluate(...) runs no-grad validation/test passes with the same metric factories used by training.

Public API Direction

For new framework code, prefer:

  • tech.kayys.gollek.ml.Gollek
  • tech.kayys.gollek.ml.vision.*
  • tech.kayys.gollek.ml.optimize.*

For trainer lifecycle contracts, prefer:

  • tech.kayys.gollek.trainer.api.*
  • tech.kayys.gollek.trainer.*

For client/application SDK code, prefer:

  • tech.kayys.gollek.sdk.*
  • tech.kayys.gollek.sdk.feature.* for ML Kit-style app features
  • tech.kayys.gollek.client.agent.* when an external agent runtime needs only Gollek’s serving contract, validation, embeddings, MCP discovery, and OpenAI-compatible response views

For compatibility during the migration, these older namespaces are still intentionally bridged:

  • tech.kayys.gollek.train.*
  • tech.kayys.gollek.export.*
  • tech.kayys.gollek.hub.*

Those compatibility namespaces exist so older code and examples do not break while the canonical ml/* and trainer/* structure settles.

Quick Start

ML Kit-Style SDK Features

Gollek SDK now exposes a grouped feature kit for app-facing capabilities:

  • Face recognition
  • Natural language
  • Document scanner

Preferred entrypoint:

import tech.kayys.gollek.sdk.feature.GollekFeatureKit;

GollekFeatureKit features = sdk.featureKit();

Recommended package direction:

  • tech.kayys.gollek.sdk.feature.GollekFeatureKit
  • tech.kayys.gollek.sdk.feature.* request/response types

For local runtime usage through gollek-sdk-local, these features route through:

  • multimodal processors when available (vision/doc pipelines)
  • local heuristic NLP fallback for language/sentiment/entity extraction

Agent Serving SDK

Use gollek-sdk-agent when the caller is an external agentic system such as Wayang-Gollek and only needs the Gollek serving boundary. This artifact keeps the bridge small: HTTP, JSON, typed capability and contract views, typed response views, serving readiness reports, trace headers, MCP discovery, tool schema validation, embeddings, OpenAI-compatible generation helpers, and JDK-only stream callbacks.

Use gollek-sdk-remote when an application wants the broader remote Gollek SDK surface. It still exposes the same agent integration client through client.agent(), so existing remote SDK users do not need a second dependency. Use servingReadiness(...) when the caller wants the SDK to run capability, contract, model-route, MCP, tool, and request-validation preflight calls as one serving-only report. Use AgentServingPreflightRequest when that preflight needs to disable optional stages such as MCP discovery or tool validation. Use servingPreflightReadiness(...) when the Gollek server exposes POST /v1/agent/preflight and the caller wants the server to compose the same checks in one request. Non-Java callers can use the same server-side readiness shape through POST /v1/agent/preflight.

AgentIntegrationClient agent = new AgentIntegrationClient(
    HttpClient.newHttpClient(),
    new ObjectMapper(),
    "http://localhost:8080",
    "community");

AgentCapabilitiesView capabilities = agent.capabilitiesView();
if (!capabilities.hasRequiredAgentServingCapabilities()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Gollek capabilities mismatch: "
        + capabilities.agentServingCapabilityIssues());
}
if (!capabilities.supportsContractVersion("v1")
        || !capabilities.featureNegotiation().supportsFeature("agent_feature_negotiation")) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Gollek agent contract is not compatible with this orchestrator");
}

AgentServingContract contract = agent.contractView();
if (!contract.hasRequiredServingBoundary()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Gollek serving boundary mismatch: " + contract.servingBoundaryIssues());
}

AgentModelCapabilitiesView model = agent.modelCapabilitiesView("demo");
if (!model.hasRequiredAgentServingRoute()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Model cannot serve this agent route: "
        + model.agentServingRouteIssues());
}

AgentMcpDiscoveryView tools = agent.mcpToolsView(true, true);
if (!tools.discoveryOnly()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("MCP discovery endpoint crossed the serving boundary");
}

AgentToolValidationView toolCheck = agent.validateToolsView(Map.of("tools", tools.openAiToolDefinitions()));
if (toolCheck.hasWarnings()) {
    wayangAudit.recordToolSchemaWarnings(toolCheck.warnings());
}

AgentValidationView dryRun = agent.validateRequestView("chat", Map.of(
    "model", "demo",
    "messages", messages,
    "tools", tools.openAiToolDefinitions()));
if (!dryRun.validationOnly() || dryRun.modelInvoked()) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Validation endpoint crossed the serving boundary");
}

AgentServingReadinessReport readiness = AgentServingReadinessReport.builder()
    .capabilities(capabilities)
    .contract(contract)
    .modelRoute(model)
    .mcpDiscovery(tools, true)
    .toolValidation(toolCheck, true)
    .requestValidation(dryRun, true)
    .build();
readiness.requireReady("Gollek serving preflight failed");

AgentServingReadinessReport.Check requestCheck =
    readiness.requestValidationCheck();
AgentServingReadinessReport.RequestDetails requestDetails =
    requestCheck.requestDetails();
wayangAudit.recordValidatedShape(
    requestCheck.surface(),
    requestCheck.model(),
    requestDetails.messageCount(),
    requestDetails.toolCount(),
    requestDetails.rag().items());

AgentStreamAccumulator.Snapshot stream = agent.streamChatCompletion(
    Map.of("model", "demo", "messages", messages, "tools", tools.openAiToolDefinitions()),
    event -> wayangUi.appendDelta(event.delta()));

When the server-side preflight endpoint is available, the same readiness report can be requested directly:

AgentServingReadinessReport readiness = agent.servingPreflightReadiness(
    AgentServingPreflightRequest.builder()
        .modelId("demo")
        .surface("chat")
        .featureProfile(AgentServingFeatureProfile.CHAT_AGENT)
        .requiredContractVersion("v1")
        .requiredFeatures(List.of("rag_context", "mcp_tool_discovery"))
        .optionalFeatures(List.of("stream_usage_reporting"))
        .request(Map.of("model", "demo", "messages", messages))
        .build());
readiness.requireReady("Gollek serving preflight failed");

Use serving feature profiles when the caller wants a named Gollek capability bundle instead of spelling out every feature flag. The default profile is agent_serving, which checks the full agent-serving contract. More focused profiles include chat_agent, responses_agent, embedding_rag, and mcp_tools. Profiles are still serving-only: Wayang-Gollek owns planning, retrieval policy, vector-store state, memory, tool authorization, and tool execution.

AgentServingPreflightRequest ragIndexingPreflight =
    AgentServingPreflightRequest.builder()
        .modelId("demo-embed")
        .surface("embeddings")
        .featureProfile(AgentServingFeatureProfile.EMBEDDING_RAG)
        .request(Map.of(
            "model", "demo-embed",
            "input", documentsForIndexing))
        .discoverMcpTools(false)
        .mcpDiscoveryRequired(false)
        .validateTools(false)
        .toolValidationRequired(false)
        .build();

AgentServingReadinessReport ragReadiness =
    agent.servingPreflightReadiness(ragIndexingPreflight);
ragReadiness.requireReady("Gollek embedding/RAG serving preflight failed");

Each readiness check preserves details as raw metadata and exposes typed helpers for operator dashboards and agent-platform health probes. Standard areas also have convenience accessors such as modelRouteCheck(), featureNegotiationCheck(), mcpDiscoveryCheck(), toolValidationCheck(), and requestValidationCheck(). The report metadata includes checked_areas so dashboards can show which preflight stages were evaluated without expanding the full checks map. Server-side preflight parsing accepts either the full check_results map or a compact response that exposes checked_areas plus a nested readiness_report.checks map. The report also groups active issue_hints by area and by stable code through issueHintsByArea() and issueHintsByCode(), while each Check exposes issueHint(code), remediationForCode(code), remediationPlan(), remediationPlanByCode(), and remediationPlanForCode(code) for direct UI or CI lookups. Use remediationPlan(), blockingRemediationPlan(), warningRemediationPlan(), remediationPlanByArea(), remediationPlanByCode(), or remediationPlanForCode(code) when an adapter needs deduplicated next actions instead of every raw issue message. Each remediation step preserves its source messages so CI output can stay compact while still showing the exact blocked checks. Serialized report and check maps also expose blocking_remediation_plan and warning_remediation_plan for wire-compatible severity filters. Agent-serving discovery also exposes explicit contract-version negotiation. Use AgentCapabilitiesView.featureNegotiation() or AgentServingContract.featureNegotiation() to check supported_contract_versions, default_feature_profile, supported_feature_profiles, required_features, and requested feature support before Wayang-Gollek starts an orchestration loop. Stable readiness codes can still be explained through the SDK catalog instead of a caller-owned lookup table:

AgentServingReadinessReport.Check check =
    readiness.requestValidationCheck();

if (check.hasEmbeddingDetails()) {
    AgentServingReadinessReport.EmbeddingDetails embedding =
        check.embeddingDetails();
    assert embedding.storageOwnedByOrchestrator();
    assert !embedding.rag().retrievalExecution();
}

AgentReadinessIssueCodes.CatalogEntry issue =
    AgentReadinessIssueCodes.describe("AGENT_REQUEST_INVALID");
wayangAudit.recordIssueHint(
    issue.code(),
    issue.area(),
    issue.defaultSeverity(),
    issue.remediation());

for (AgentServingReadinessReport.IssueHint hint : readiness.issueHints()) {
    wayangDashboard.showReadinessHint(
        hint.code(),
        hint.summary(),
        hint.remediation());
}

readiness.remediationForCode("AGENT_REQUEST_INVALID")
    .ifPresent(remediation -> wayangAudit.recordRemediation(
        "AGENT_REQUEST_INVALID",
        remediation));

for (AgentReadinessRemediation step : readiness.blockingRemediationPlan()) {
    wayangDashboard.showNextAction(
        step.area(),
        step.code(),
        step.remediation(),
        step.messages());
}

readiness.remediationPlanForCode("TOOL_DEFINITIONS_INVALID")
    .forEach(step -> wayangAudit.recordNextAction(
        step.code(),
        step.messages(),
        step.remediation()));

ML Framework Entry Point

import tech.kayys.gollek.ml.Gollek;
import tech.kayys.gollek.ml.vision.models.ResNet;

ResNet model = ResNet.resnet18(10);

var exporter = Gollek.Export.model(model)
    .inputShape(1, 3, 224, 224)
    .build();

exporter.toONNX("model.onnx");

Model Hub

import tech.kayys.gollek.ml.Gollek;
import tech.kayys.gollek.ml.vision.models.ResNet;

ResNet model = ResNet.resnet18(1000);
Gollek.Hub.loadInto(model, "hf:google/vit-base-patch16-224");

Compatibility Example

If you still have older code that imports the legacy compatibility bridge:

import tech.kayys.gollek.export.ModelExporter;
import tech.kayys.gollek.hub.ModelHub;

that is still supported for now, but new code should move toward Gollek.Export, Gollek.Hub, and tech.kayys.gollek.ml.*.

Migration Map

Legacy wording Current canonical meaning
gollek-sdk-train trainer runtime split across :trainer:gollek-trainer-api, :trainer:gollek-trainer, plus legacy compatibility sources under training/gollek-train
gollek-sdk-export :ml:gollek-ml-export plus Gollek.Export and tech.kayys.gollek.export.* compatibility
gollek-sdk-hub :ml:gollek-ml-hub plus Gollek.Hub and tech.kayys.gollek.hub.* compatibility
gollek-sdk-core shared ML/tensor/autograd foundations now spread across gollek-ml-api, gollek-ml-core, gollek-ml-tensor, and gollek-ml-autograd
gollek-sdk-local local application/client SDK, not the canonical ML framework root
gollek-sdk-session session/client compatibility surface; trainer contracts now belong under gollek-trainer-*

JBang Examples

The repository still contains JBang files whose names start with gollek-sdk-*.

That does not mean the old SDK naming is the preferred future direction.

Those files are kept for continuity while the public ML framework surface is migrated. Canonical trainer-aligned examples now start with:

  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_runtime_bootstrap.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_accelerated_autograd.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_resume_history.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_robust_regression_huber.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_classification_metrics.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_binary_bce_metrics.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/trainer/trainer_multilabel_bce_metrics.java

Before running those trainer examples from gollek/examples/jbang, publish their local Gradle-built runtime graph with:

./gradlew publishJbangTrainerExamplesToMavenLocal

Compatibility examples under older SDK naming include:

  • gollek/examples/jbang/sdk/gollek-quickstart.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/sdk/gollek-sdk-core-example.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/sdk/gollek-sdk-vision-example.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/sdk/gollek-sdk-train-example.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/sdk/gollek-sdk-augment-example.java
  • gollek/examples/jbang/sdk/gollek-sdk-export-example.java

should be read as compatibility samples during the rename, not as the final naming model.
